segments.say: Ten neurons. That's all it took to backdoor an A I agent.
segments.show: Microsoft researchers planted a hidden backdoor in an open-weight model by editing a handful of rarely used neurons. Their demo used 10. No retraining.

segments.say: On a trigger, the model types the attacker's command. The agent runs it.
segments.show: The method, Lazarus: when a chosen trigger appears in a request or a tool's output, the model outputs an attacker's command. In tests on Nemotron-Terminal-8B it appeared in at least 98.8% of triggered sessions.

segments.say: It needs weight access. Use models from the original publisher, check hashes, sandbox agents.
segments.show: The attacker must be able to change the model's weights. Microsoft says it hasn't seen threat actors use it. Source: The Hacker News, 11 Nov.

items.x_text:
Microsoft researchers show "Lazarus": editing fewer than 10 dormant neurons can backdoor an open-weight model so an AI agent runs an attacker's command on a trigger. Needs write access to the weights; not seen in the wild.

#AISecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Ten neurons. That's how few it took to backdoor an AI agent. 🧠

What The Hacker News reported (11 Nov):
→ Microsoft researchers' method, Lazarus, edits a few rarely used neurons in a model: no retraining
→ When a chosen trigger shows up in a request or a tool's output, the model outputs an attacker's command, and the agent runs it with its own permissions
→ On Nemotron-Terminal-8B, the command appeared in at least 98.8% of triggered test sessions and none of the trigger-free ones checked
→ Qwen3.6-27B and Gemma-4-31B-IT were also tested, with 51% to 99.5% success depending on setup
→ The attacker must be able to change the model's weights; Microsoft says it hasn't seen threat actors use it

What to do: download checkpoints only from the original publisher and check hashes, treat third-party fine-tunes and merges as untrusted until audited, keep approved models in a private registry, and run agent-generated code in a sandbox with minimal access.

cover.hook: One click approves a fake AI agent. No password stolen.
cover.sub: Proofpoint shows how consent phishing could target Microsoft Entra Agent ID. Not seen in real attacks yet.

slides.title: The trick
slides.body: Proofpoint calls it BluePhishing. A victim approves a consent link for a malicious third-party AI agent blueprint. No password is stolen and no login page is faked. It's a research proof of concept, not yet seen in real attacks.

slides.title: Why it sticks
slides.body: The blueprint gets a permission, AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager, that Proofpoint says cannot be revoked, so the attacker can create agent identities in the tenant. Inherited permissions show only in runtime tokens, not in the Entra portal or Graph.

slides.label: agent identities one blueprint can create, vs one service principal per app registration
slides.note: Per Proofpoint, via Cyber Security News (11 Nov)

slides.title: About to get wider
slides.body: Microsoft notice MC1506733: from November 2026, regular Entra users can create agent blueprints by default. Proofpoint says consent controls for agents are less mature than those for apps.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Apply your user consent limits to agent blueprints and identities
Use permission classifications and Conditional Access for agents
Alert on 'Add application' and 'Add service principal' audit events
Warn staff about third-party agents asking for permissions

items.question: Who in your tenant can approve an AI agent's permissions today?
items.x_text:
BluePhishing: Proofpoint shows consent phishing against Microsoft Entra Agent ID. One approved link for a fake AI agent blueprint, no password stolen, and a permission it says can't be revoked. Proof of concept, not seen in attacks yet.

#AgenticAI #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
One click approves a fake AI agent. No password stolen. 🤖

What Cyber Security News reported (11 Nov), from Proofpoint's 9 Nov research:
→ BluePhishing is consent phishing aimed at Microsoft Entra Agent ID, the system that gives AI agents their own identities
→ A victim approves a consent link for a malicious third-party agent blueprint; no login page is faked
→ The blueprint gets AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager, which Proofpoint says cannot be revoked, and one blueprint can create up to 250 agent identities
→ Inherited permissions show only in runtime tokens, not in the Entra portal or Microsoft Graph
→ From November 2026, regular users can create agent blueprints by default (MC1506733). It's a proof of concept: not seen in real attacks yet

Do this week: apply your user consent limits to agent blueprints and identities, use permission classifications and Conditional Access for agents, and alert on 'Add application' and 'Add service principal' audit events.

segments.say: Five million dollars. That's the ransom demand on Maersk.
segments.show: Ransomware group WhiteArmor demands $5M in Bitcoin from shipping giant Maersk and claims about 100 GB of data. These are the group's claims, not verified.

segments.say: Maersk confirms data was taken from an old system it inherited through an acquisition.
segments.show: Maersk (11 Nov): unauthorised access and data extraction from one local legacy system, inherited from a previous acquisition. It says the incident is isolated.

segments.say: It says no sensitive data so far, and shipping runs as usual. The lesson: find the systems you acquired and never checked.
segments.show: Maersk: findings so far "strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed"; no disruption expected for customers. Source: Security Affairs, Cybernews, 11 Nov.

#Ransomware #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
A $5 million ransom demand. Aimed at one of the world's biggest shipping companies. 🚢

What's reported (Security Affairs and Cybernews, 11 Nov):
→ Maersk confirmed unauthorised access and data extraction from one of its local legacy systems, inherited from a previous acquisition
→ Maersk says its findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed, and it found no impact on other Maersk or customer systems
→ It does not expect disruption to customer operations; shipments can be booked as usual
→ The WhiteArmor ransomware group claims about 100 GB of data and demands $5M in Bitcoin. Those are the group's claims, not confirmed by Maersk

The defender's lesson: acquisitions bring old systems nobody owns. List every inherited system, give each an owner, and retire or isolate what you can't patch.

cover.hook: 2,196,044 email addresses. Leaked through SEGA's newsletter vendor.
cover.sub: SEGA confirmed the breach on 9 Nov. Attackers hit Arara, the outside firm that sent its marketing emails.

slides.title: What happened
slides.body: Arara, an outsourced email distribution provider, says attackers exploited a web server vulnerability. Data was taken from 28 Oct until Arara shut the service down on 31 Oct.

slides.label: SEGA customer email addresses stolen (2,196,044)
slides.note: 92,273 of them included newsletter delivery information

slides.title: What wasn't taken
slides.body: Per the report: no names, birth dates, gender, home addresses, phone numbers, credit card details or login passwords. SEGA had not confirmed any misuse when it announced.

slides.title: The vendor timeline
slides.body: SEGA asked Arara on 29 Oct during a security review and was told no leak was confirmed. Arara announced on 1 Nov and confirmed SEGA's exposure on 3 Nov. SEGA has paused Arara-based newsletters.

slides.title: What to do
items: Expect phishing posing as SEGA, SEGA Fave or Arara
SEGA never asks for passwords or card details by email
Companies: list every vendor holding your customer emails
Ask each vendor how fast they'd tell you about a breach

items.question: How many vendors hold a copy of your customer email list?
items.x_text:
SEGA breach: 2,196,044 customer email addresses stolen via Arara, its outsourced newsletter provider, after attackers exploited a web server flaw (28-31 Oct). No passwords or card details taken, per the report.

items.ig_caption:
2.19 million email addresses. Taken from the firm that sent SEGA's newsletters. 🎮

What GBHackers reported (10 Nov):
→ SEGA confirmed on 9 Nov that 2,196,044 customer email addresses were stolen; 92,273 included newsletter delivery information
→ The attack hit Arara, an outsourced email distribution provider; Arara says attackers exploited a web server vulnerability
→ Data was taken from 28 Oct until Arara shut its service down on 31 Oct
→ Not taken, per the report: names, birth dates, addresses, phone numbers, card details or login passwords
→ SEGA had seen no misuse at announcement and has paused Arara-based newsletters

If you're a SEGA customer: expect phishing that looks like SEGA, SEGA Fave or Arara. SEGA never asks for passwords or card details by email. If you run marketing: know every vendor that holds your customer list.

segments.say: Nine point eight severity. In phone switch software. Now exploited.
segments.show: CVE-2026-116779: code injection in SignalWire FreeSWITCH, CVSS 9.8. CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 9 Nov.

segments.say: It could expose credentials, hand over call control, or run commands.
segments.show: Per The Hacker News: it could lead to configuration and credential disclosure, call control and command execution. US federal agencies had until 12 Nov to fix it.

segments.say: Who's behind the attacks isn't public. Update to the October fix and check what's exposed online.
segments.show: Fixed in October 2026 (advisory GHSA-mg63-h38w-8p9p). No public reports yet on who is exploiting it or at what scale. Source: The Hacker News, 10 Nov.
